newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. peacekeepers will leave Haiti on July 31.
newsitem.headline: U.N. peacekeepers will leave Haiti on July 31.

text.p: Security Council members said on Thursday that U.N. peacekeepers would remain in Haiti at their current strength until July 31 and then leave the Caribbean nation.

The council, in informal discussions, approved a recent recommendation by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan to keep the present complement of 500 U.N. troops and 262 civilian police in the Caribbean nation until their mandate expires for a final time on July 31.
Diplomats said there would be no discussion about extending the U.N. peacekeeping mandate longer than that.

Council President Pedro Catarino of Portugal said members agreed with Annan's report and said the "climate of violence and insecurity" made it imperative to keep the the U.N. units there at current strength until the mandate expires. Fifty people have been killed over the last two months.
Envoys said there was usually a grace period after a mandate ended for force levels to be drawn down, which meant the troops would begin leaving early in August.
Annan will make a recommendation in June on the shape of U.N. civilian operations in Haiti, including the current human rights monitoring unit as well as development assistance officials.

Canada intends to keep troops and police forces in Haiti past the U.N. deadline and until the end of 1997, Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said last month. But the Canadian cabinet has not taken a final decision on the issue, although the force is likely to be half of the 750 soldiers it currently has in Haiti.
About 422 Canadians are funded by U.N. members, while another 300, along with 500 Pakistani troops, are mandated outside the U.N. structure and paid for by Canada and the United States.
Ottawa can keep its troops in Haiti on a request from Haiti's President Rene Preval and without U.N. approval, although it may want the Security Council to give its blessing to a continued presence.

China and Russia have opposed any extension of the U.N. peacekeeping mission, arguing that development aid is needed instead. In exchange for renewing the force over the past year, Bejing had insisted on a reduction of numbers.
To make up the difference, Canada has been paying for most of its own troops.

One of the operation's main tasks was to train and monitor Haiti's fledgling police, which replaced the previous paramilitary contingents loyal to the military junta that overthrew elected President Jean-Bertrand Aristide in 1991.

He was restored to power three years later by a U.S.-led 22,000-member multinational force. The United Nations took over peacekeeping in March 1995 with 6,000 troops, a number that has been steadily reduced since then.

In December the council agreed to extend the mission for a final time until May 31, subject to renewal for another two months until July 31. But Security Council sources said the United States had argued no new resolution was needed to keep the force there until the July 31 date.
